title: A regular sequence at a prime spreads to a principal neighbourhood
statement: Let $R$ be a commutative Noetherian ring [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring], let $\mathfrak p\subset R$ be a prime ideal, and let $r\ge0$ and $x_1,\ldots,x_r\in R$. If their images form a regular sequence [def-weil-pbc-regular-sequence] in the localization $R_{\mathfrak p}$ [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime], then there exists $g\in R\setminus\mathfrak p$ such that their images form a regular sequence in the principal localization $R[1/g]$ [def-weil-ring-localization-away].

source.place: Tag 061L, lemma-regular-sequence-in-neighbourhood, specializing the finite module M to R.

proof.text: For $0\leq i\leq r$, put $I_i=(x_1,\ldots,x_i)$ and $Q_i=R/I_i$, with $I_0=(0)$. For $1\leq i\leq r$, let $K_i=\ker(x_i:Q_{i-1}\to Q_{i-1})$. Each $Q_{i-1}$ is generated as an $R$-module by the class of $1$. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-noetherian-submodule-finite] to this finite module and its submodule $K_i$: every $K_i$ has a finite list of generators. The only finiteness hypothesis used here is that $R$ is Noetherian.

source.place: Tag 061L, lemma-regular-sequence-in-neighbourhood, proof: definition and finiteness of K_i; Tag 00IK, lemma-Noetherian-basic, second assertion

proof.text: For either $T=R\setminus\mathfrak p$ or $T=\{1,g,g^2,\ldots\}$, apply [lem-weil-pbc-localization-module-exact] to $0\to I_i\to R\to Q_i\to0$. It identifies $T^{-1}Q_i$ with $(T^{-1}R)/(x_1/1,\ldots,x_i/1)$: the map sends $(a+I_i)/t$ to the class of $a/t$. Indeed the localized quotient map $q_T:T^{-1}R\to T^{-1}Q_i$, $a/t\mapsto(a+I_i)/t$, is surjective by lifting numerators, and exactness gives $\ker q_T=\operatorname{im}(T^{-1}I_i\to T^{-1}R)$. This image is precisely the ideal generated by the $x_j/1$, so $q_T$ induces a bijection from the quotient by that ideal; its inverse is the displayed map. To check this last equality, write $a=\sum_j b_jx_j$ for an element of $I_i$; then $a/t=\sum_j(b_j/t)(x_j/1)$. Conversely a finite sum of multiples of $x_j/1$ has a common denominator in $T$ and numerator in $I_i$. Surjectivity follows by lifting the numerator of each fraction. These identifications intertwine multiplication by every $x_j$, directly from the fraction formula in [def-weil-pbc-module-localization]. The two choices of $T$ give exactly the prime and principal localizations in [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime] and [def-weil-ring-localization-away].

source.place: Tag 061L, lemma-regular-sequence-in-neighbourhood, proof: localization of the successive quotients; Tag 00CS, proposition-localization-exact

proof.text: Localize $0\to K_i\to Q_{i-1}\xrightarrow{x_i}Q_{i-1}$ at $R\setminus\mathfrak p$. By [lem-weil-pbc-localization-module-exact], the localized inclusion of $K_i$ is injective and its image is the kernel of multiplication by $x_i/1$. Under the quotient identification in step 2, that multiplication is injective by the assumed regularity and [def-weil-pbc-regular-sequence]. Its kernel is zero, so $(K_i)_{\mathfrak p}=0$ for every $i$.

source.place: Tag 061L, lemma-regular-sequence-in-neighbourhood, proof: each K_i has zero localization at p; Tag 00CS

proof.text: Choose finite generators $k_{i1},\ldots,k_{in_i}$ of each $K_i$ from step 1. Since $k_{ij}/1=0$ in $(K_i)_{\mathfrak p}$, the zero criterion in [def-weil-pbc-module-localization] supplies $s_{ij}\notin\mathfrak p$ with $s_{ij}k_{ij}=0$. Let $g=\prod_{i,j}s_{ij}$, using $g=1$ if the indexing set is empty. Primality implies $g\notin\mathfrak p$. Every $s_{ij}$ divides $g$, so $gk_{ij}=0$; writing an arbitrary element as a linear combination of the generators gives $gK_i=0$. Thus every fraction $k/g^n$ in $(K_i)_g$ is zero, by the same localization zero criterion with multiplier $g$. This proves $(K_i)_g=0$ simultaneously, including the case $r=0$.

source.place: Tag 061L, lemma-regular-sequence-in-neighbourhood, proof: choose a common g annihilating the finite kernels; the generator argument is written out

proof.text: Apply [lem-weil-pbc-localization-module-exact] again to $K_i\to Q_{i-1}\xrightarrow{x_i}Q_{i-1}$, now at the powers of $g$. Step 4 makes the localized left term zero, so multiplication by $x_i/1$ on $(Q_{i-1})_g$ has zero kernel. The explicit identifications of step 2 therefore show that $x_i/1$ is a nonzerodivisor on $R[1/g]/(x_1/1,\ldots,x_{i-1}/1)$ for every $i$.

source.place: Tag 061L, lemma-regular-sequence-in-neighbourhood, proof: this g works, nonzerodivisor condition; Tag 00CS

proof.text: It remains to check the nonzero-quotient condition of [def-weil-pbc-regular-sequence]. Every $x_i$ lies in $\mathfrak p$: otherwise its inverse in the fraction construction [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime] is $1/x_i$, making the final quotient there zero, contrary to the assumed regularity. If $1$ belonged to $(x_1/1,\ldots,x_r/1)$ in $R[1/g]$, write $1=\sum_i(b_i/g^{n_i})(x_i/1)$. Choose $N\geq n_i$ for every $i$ (and $N=0$ for the empty list), and set $a_i=b_i g^{N-n_i}$. The fraction addition and multiplication formulas give $1=(\sum_i a_ix_i)/g^N$. The equality criterion of [def-weil-ring-localization-away] then gives $g^k(g^N-\sum_i a_ix_i)=0$ for some $k\geq0$. Hence $g^{N+k}\in\mathfrak p$, impossible because $g\notin\mathfrak p$ and $\mathfrak p$ is prime and proper. Thus the final quotient is nonzero. For $r=0$ the same argument uses the empty sum and $g=1$, so it also proves the assertion for the empty sequence. Combining this with step 5 is precisely regularity in $R[1/g]$.
